name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,285

clue.text: Army chap destroyed source of drugs

indicators.note: something destroyed is broken apart, so the letters must be rebuilt in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A soldier has wrecked a supplier of narcotics, like a raid on a drug lord's lab.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Army chap' looks like one soldier, but the two words are simply the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A chemist's shop is where medicines are dispensed, so it is literally a place you obtain medication from.

clue.text: Mountain, say, cut off at the top

indicators.note: in a down entry the top is the start, so the opening letter is chopped away

blocks.note: to say something is to speak it

explanation.surface: A mountain whose summit has been sheared off, perhaps by erosion.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'at the top' means the first letter, so the S goes and PEAK is left.
explanation.definitionFit: A peak is a pointed summit, and by extension a whole mountain, as in the high peaks of the Rockies.

clue.text: Surprise tons with a noise outside

indicators.note: one thing sitting outside another wraps around it

blocks.note: taken as written
any noise is a sound
T is the abbreviation for tons

explanation.surface: Something huge and very loud gives everyone a shock, like tons of rubble crashing down.
explanation.walkthrough: The noise word wraps around the tons abbreviation, with A in front: A + S(T)OUND.
explanation.definitionFit: To astound someone is to amaze or shock them greatly, a stronger synonym for catching them off guard.

clue.text: Two fish pierced by tip of sharp metal implement

indicators.note: whatever is pierced has something pushed into it, so a piece goes inside
the tip of a word is its very first letter

blocks.note: two fish, the marlin and the pike, one after the other
first letter of sharp

explanation.surface: Two fish are skewered by a pointed metal tool, like catch on a spit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two fish' gives two separate words, split around the single letter. A marlinspike is a pointed tool sailors use to separate strands of rope when splicing.
explanation.definitionFit: A marlinspike is a tapered steel spike used in ropework and splicing, so it is a metal tool.

clue.text: Crowd in church with English dress

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

blocks.note: CH is the abbreviation for church
a lot is a group or crowd of people
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A congregation at church is wearing its English finery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dress' reads as a noun in the surface, but here it is the verb: C(LOT)H + E.
explanation.definitionFit: To dress someone is to put garments on them, which is exactly what the verb clothe means.

clue.text: X in “waXwork” is supersized

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the words that follow, spanning their letters

blocks.note: run across the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A quip about a wax museum, where the capital letter in the middle of the word has been blown up in size.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital X in the quoted word is a decoy, drawing the eye; the definition is the X at the start, the letter-writer's sign for a smooch.
explanation.definitionFit: Letter writers sign off with a row of crosses meaning smooches, so the cross symbol stands for that affectionate gesture.

clue.text: Inadequate IT holds author up

indicators.note: in a down entry going up means reading from bottom to top, backwards
to hold something is to keep it within, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: taken as written
to author a work is to pen it

explanation.surface: A useless IT department keeps a writer waiting, holding up their work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holds up' reads as delaying, but the phrase splits: 'holds' puts one piece inside IT, and 'up' flips that piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Inept means lacking skill or competence, a close synonym of inadequate when describing performance.

clue.text: Mailing involving poster initially paying out

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word before it
to involve something is to take it in, so a piece goes inside

blocks.note: mailing a letter is sending it
first letter of poster

explanation.surface: A mailshot with a poster in it costs the sender money.
explanation.walkthrough: S(P)ENDING: the single letter slips in after the first letter of the mailing word.
explanation.definitionFit: Spending is laying out money, the same as paying it out for goods or services.

clue.text: Trying to find roof beam when the first goes missing

indicators.note: the first of a word going missing means its opening letter is dropped

blocks.note: a rafter is a sloping beam that supports a roof

explanation.surface: Someone is searching for a roof beam after the first one has vanished.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the R from the roof beam. 'After' here is the sense in 'the police are after him'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being after something means pursuing or seeking it, as in chasing a goal or a suspect.

clue.text: Bad smell around place is disgusting

indicators.note: turning something around makes it face the other way, so it reads backwards

blocks.note: BO is body odour
a scene is the place where something happens

explanation.surface: A foul stink hanging about somewhere is revolting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' looks like a container signal wrapping the smell around the place, but it only turns the smell backwards; BO is the standard shorthand for body odour.
explanation.definitionFit: Obscene means offensive to accepted standards of decency, so repulsive or revolting in a strong sense.

clue.text: Secondary route Sinbad organised

indicators.note: to organise is to put into a fresh arrangement, so the letters get reordered

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A back road planned by Sinbad, the legendary sailor, for one of his voyages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Secondary route' reads as one phrase, a side road, but the definition is the first word alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Something subordinate is lower in rank or importance, which is what secondary means.

clue.text: Wanton unoccupied suffering change of heart in favour of one

indicators.text: suffering change of heart in favour of
indicators.note: a change of heart swaps out the central letter for something else

blocks.note: a place nobody lives in is unoccupied
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: An empty-headed wanton has a change of heart and decides to settle for one partner.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle letter of the eleven-letter word for unoccupied is A; swap it for I.
explanation.definitionFit: Wanton can mean unrestrained or free of moral restraint, and uninhibited describes someone without such restraint.

clue.text: Alternative to rice cold? Often it’s cooked

indicators.note: cooked means doctored or fiddled, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps
taken as written

explanation.surface: A kitchen musing: cold food as a substitute for rice, which is usually served hot.
explanation.walkthrough: Rice and paper pieces are both thrown over couples leaving a wedding, which is the sense of 'alternative' here.
explanation.definitionFit: Guests traditionally shower newlyweds with grains or paper scraps, so the paper version replaces the grains.

clue.text: Getting on, feeling the chill a bit without cape

indicators.note: without means lacking, so a letter is taken away

blocks.note: somewhat cold
C is the map abbreviation for cape

explanation.surface: An ageing person starts to feel the cold a little when they leave their cloak off.
explanation.walkthrough: A cape reads as a cloak, but it is the headland abbreviation C, removed from the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone getting on is ageing, and oldish describes a person who is fairly advanced in years.

clue.text: Cowardly Charlie chased by bird

blocks.note: C is Charlie in the NATO phonetic alphabet
a raven is a large black bird

explanation.surface: A timid man named Charlie flees from a pursuing bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chased by' means followed by, so the bird comes after C.
explanation.definitionFit: Craven is an old-fashioned word for contemptibly lacking courage, a direct synonym of cowardly.

clue.text: Struggle introducing new label showing year wine’s made

indicators.note: to introduce something is to bring it inside

blocks.note: to vie is to compete or struggle
N is the abbreviation for new
a tag is a label

explanation.surface: A winery wrestles over a new bottle label giving the year of production.
explanation.walkthrough: VI(N TAG)E: the struggle word opens to take in the new label.
explanation.definitionFit: A wine's vintage is the year its grapes were harvested and the wine was produced.

clue.text: Rook cat’s chewed and half left

indicators.note: chewed means mangled, so the letters are jumbled
keeping only half of a word means losing the rest of it

blocks.note: taken as written without the apostrophe
taken as written; its first half is kept

explanation.surface: A cat has mauled a crow-like bird and left half of it behind.
explanation.walkthrough: Rook looks like the bird the cat caught, but it is the chess piece.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess the rook is also called the castle, since the piece is shaped like a tower.

clue.text: Lure of saint leaving Italy in 1922-43?

indicators.note: something leaving departs, so those letters are taken out

blocks.note: Italy under Mussolini, from 1922 to 1943, was a Fascist state
ST is the abbreviation for saint

explanation.surface: A holy man's attraction to leaving Mussolini's Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: The dates are those of Mussolini's rule; remove ST from the phrase describing the country then.
explanation.definitionFit: A lure is a powerful attraction, and fascination is the state of being strongly drawn or captivated.

clue.text: Small price paid for renting horse

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as in clothing sizes
hire is the fee paid to rent something

explanation.surface: A modest fee to rent a horse for a ride.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the last word; the rest builds the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A shire is a very large, strong English breed of draught animal used for pulling heavy loads.

clue.text: Animal running up for grass

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top, backwards

blocks.note: a deer is an animal

explanation.surface: An animal bounds uphill looking for grazing.
explanation.walkthrough: The animal is a DEER, which in this down entry is written bottom to top.
explanation.definitionFit: Reeds are tall water plants of the grass family, so a reed is a kind of grass.

clue.text: Spear I had found in river

indicators.note: something found in another lies inside it

blocks.note: the Trent is a major river in the English Midlands
I'd is the contraction of I had

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to discovering a spear in a riverbed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'River' is not the usual crossword R here but the Trent, a long river in central England.
explanation.definitionFit: A trident is a three-pronged spear, like the one carried by Neptune or used for fishing.

clue.text: Head of arboretum donated succulent

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: first letter of arboretum
to donate is to give, so donated is gave

explanation.surface: The director of a tree garden has given away a fleshy plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Succulent' reads as an adjective in the surface, but it is the noun for a fleshy plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Agave is a spiky desert plant with thick fleshy leaves, the source of tequila, and so a succulent.

clue.text: I encountered returning pair of lovers

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came, so it reads backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
to encounter someone is to meet them

explanation.surface: Someone recalls bumping into a couple on their way home.
explanation.walkthrough: The couple in the clue is the definition, not someone you met.
explanation.definitionFit: Two people described as an item are in a romantic relationship, an informal idiom for a couple.

clue.text: Clergyman always gripped by right objective

indicators.note: whatever is gripped is held inside something else

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right
ever means always, as in ever hopeful
an end is an aim or objective

explanation.surface: A minister who is forever in the grip of righteous aims.
explanation.walkthrough: The right-hand letter and the objective together hold the word for always: R(EVER)END.
explanation.definitionFit: Reverend is the title and informal name for a member of the clergy, such as a minister or priest.
